front: What is an interval estimate for a parameter?
back: A range of values, calculated from sample data, that is likely to contain the true value of the population parameter, rather than a single point value.

front: What is the formula for the approximate confidence interval for a population proportion p?
back: (p̂ − z√(p̂(1−p̂)/n), p̂ + z√(p̂(1−p̂)/n)), where p̂ is the sample proportion, n is the sample size, and z is the appropriate quantile for the standard normal distribution.

front: In the confidence interval formula for p, what does z represent?
back: The appropriate quantile for the standard normal distribution corresponding to the chosen level of confidence.

front: What is the formula for the approximate margin of error when estimating a population proportion?
What does the margin of error represent in a confidence interval for a proportion?
back: The maximum likely distance between the sample proportion p̂ and the true population proportion p, at a given level of confidence — it determines the half-width of the confidence interval.

front: How does increasing the level of confidence affect the margin of error, all else being equal?
back: Increasing the level of confidence increases z, which increases the margin of error, producing a wider confidence interval.

front: How does increasing the sample size n affect the margin of error, all else being equal?
back: Increasing n decreases the margin of error (since n appears under the square root in the denominator), producing a narrower confidence interval.

front: If many different random samples are taken and a 95% confidence interval is constructed from each, what proportion of these intervals would be expected to contain the true population proportion p?
back: Approximately 95% of the intervals would contain p, meaning most, but not all, confidence intervals constructed this way will capture the true population proportion — intervals vary from sample to sample.
